behavior_text: The threat actor identified a Modicon PLC whose web-based management interface was directly reachable from the public internet. After enumerating the exposed device, they exploited an authentication-bypass flaw in that web application to gain an initial foothold on the controller without any valid credentials.

Having gained access to the engineering workstation, the adversary used the vendor's programming software to download modified ladder logic to the target PLC. The tampered program altered the control routine so that the pump would continue running past its safe operating threshold.

Initial access was achieved through a spearphishing email sent to a control-systems engineer. The message carried a weaponized spreadsheet attachment; when the engineer opened the file and enabled macros, a loader executed and established a foothold on the OT network.

To disrupt operations, the actor directed a flood of malformed packets at the safety controller, exhausting its network stack until it became unresponsive. With the device offline, operators at the HMI could no longer observe live process values, producing a sustained loss of view.

After establishing control over the distributed control system, the adversary raised alarm thresholds well beyond normal operating ranges and disabled several critical process alarms entirely. This ensured that as they manipulated the process, operators received no warning of the abnormal conditions.

The intrusion began with valid VPN credentials harvested from an earlier IT-network compromise. Using these legitimate accounts, the actor connected through the utility's external remote-access service directly into the OT environment, blending in with normal administrator activity.

Positioned on the process network, the actor passively captured Modbus/TCP traffic between the master and field devices to learn the polling structure. They then inserted themselves into the communication path, altering setpoint values in transit before the messages reached the RTU.

With engineering access to the controller, the adversary changed calibration parameters governing a chemical dosing pump, pushing the flow setpoint outside safe bounds. The manipulation drove the physical process into an unsafe state while readings on the operator console still appeared nominal.

The group loaded unsigned, malicious firmware onto a safety instrumented system controller. The tampered firmware disabled the SIS's protective trip functions, creating the potential for a loss of safety should a hazardous process condition arise.

An infected contractor laptop, a transient cyber asset periodically connected to the plant's engineering workstation, carried malware into the otherwise segmented OT network. Once connected, the malware spread to removable USB media used to shuttle files between air-gapped systems.

For several weeks leading up to the incident, the historian logged repeated read-only polling from an unfamiliar host during off-hours, alongside a slow, methodical sweep that appeared to touch nearly every address on the plant subnet.
When operators tried to open the discharge valve from the control room, the interface reported the command had gone through, yet the valve position never actually changed.
Even as the tank's physical level dropped toward empty, the reading on the operator's screen held steady at a comfortable two-thirds full for the better part of an hour.

An account normally limited to viewing HMI screens was somehow able to push a firmware update to a field controller, and the order in which the automation sequence ran its steps came out rearranged afterward, with a safety interlock now executing last instead of first.
Outbound connections from the engineering laptop were indistinguishable from ordinary web browsing at a glance, using the same familiar ports the rest of the office traffic already relied on.
A relief valve stayed shut well past the pressure it was rated to release at, and the vessel behind it eventually gave way.
